concepts.text: AI questions test a few families of facts again and again: agent and environment classifications, the properties of each search algorithm, logic and probability rules, learning formulas and the update rules of neural networks. The tables below gather them in syllabus order. Use this sheet for last-minute revision; every entry is explained with worked examples in its subtopic.

Taxi driving is partially observable, stochastic, sequential, dynamic, continuous and multi-agent; a crossword is fully observable, deterministic, static and single-agent.

concepts.plainText: A*: path cost so far plus heuristic; h admissible if it never overestimates the true cost h*

items: Hill climbing stalls at local maxima, plateaux and ridges; random restarts and simulated annealing (accept worse moves with probability e^(−ΔE/T)) help.
CSP heuristics: MRV picks the variable with fewest legal values, the degree heuristic breaks ties, LCV orders values; forward checking and arc consistency (AC-3) prune domains.
Minimax: MAX takes the largest child value, MIN the smallest. Alpha-beta prunes branches that cannot affect the decision; perfect ordering gives O(b^(m/2)).
Semantic nets link concepts with IS-A and instance arcs so properties are inherited; frames group slots with facets such as value, default and if-needed demons.
FOPL resolution refutation: negate the goal, convert to clausal form (Skolemise existentials, drop universals), unify with the most general unifier, and derive the empty clause.
Forward chaining is data-driven (facts → conclusions); backward chaining is goal-driven (goal → supporting facts), as in MYCIN.

notes.text: Numeric questions here are mostly: node counts for BFS/IDS/bidirectional search, A* and minimax/alpha-beta traces, entropy and information gain, Bayes posteriors, fuzzy min/max values, roulette-wheel probabilities, neuron outputs and one-step weight updates. Write the formula before substituting.

Easy swaps: admissible (never overestimates) vs consistent (triangle inequality); DFS (stack) vs BFS (queue); forward (data-driven) vs backward (goal-driven) chaining; perceptron (t − y) vs Adaline (t − net); Mamdani (fuzzy outputs) vs Sugeno (crisp functions).
A single-layer perceptron only separates linearly separable classes, so it cannot learn XOR; one hidden layer trained with backpropagation can.

formulas.title: Entropy
formulas.description: Zero for a pure sample and 1 bit for an even two-class split; ID3 splits on the attribute with the largest gain.

formulas.title: Perceptron rule

flashcards.front: What is the space complexity of iterative deepening search?
flashcards.back: O(bd), linear like DFS, while keeping BFS's completeness and optimality for unit step costs.

flashcards.front: What are the fuzzy AND, OR and NOT operators?
flashcards.back: AND is the minimum, OR is the maximum and NOT is 1 minus the membership value.

flashcards.front: What is the derivative of the sigmoid function in terms of its output?
flashcards.back: σ'(x) = σ(x)(1 − σ(x)), which is at most 0.25 (at x = 0).

questions.questionText: Which pairing of technique and learning paradigm is correct?
questions.explanation: Q-learning learns action values from rewards, which is reinforcement learning; K-means is unsupervised, while ID3 and naive Bayes learn from labelled examples (supervised).

A Bayesian network has three Boolean variables with edges A → B and A → C. How many independent probabilities do its conditional probability tables need, compared with 7 for the full joint distribution?
questions.explanation: P(A) needs 1 value, and P(B | A) and P(C | A) need 2 each (one per value of A): 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, versus 2³ − 1 = 7 for the full joint table.

questions.questionText: A disease affects 1% of people. A test detects it 90% of the time and gives a false positive for 5% of healthy people. If a person tests positive, the probability that they have the disease is about:
questions.explanation: P(D|+) = 0.01·0.9 / (0.01·0.9 + 0.99·0.05) = 0.009 / 0.0585 ≈ 0.154, because healthy false positives far outnumber true positives.

questions.questionText: Which expert-system component tells the user why a question is being asked and how a conclusion was reached?
questions.explanation: The explanation facility answers 'why' and 'how' queries by tracing the rules the inference engine used, which builds user trust.
